title: Date codes and era rules
summary: How to read YYWW and capacitor date codes on salvaged parts, and the dates when solder, refrigerants, PCBs, mercury, smoke-alarm sources, CRT glass, asbestos and cadmium change what is inside. Each date is given with its source.

steps.text: Read the date codes on several parts and take the newest: that is roughly when the device was made.
Check the device against the table before you open it: old ballasts, motor capacitors, thermostats, CRTs and asbestos parts need care.
steps.warn: Assume an unmarked, undated capacitor from before 1979 holds PCBs. Never break a mercury switch or a CRT.

notes:
## Reading a date code
- **Four digits, YYWW:** year, then week. 9948 is week 48 of 1999. 2333 is week 33 of 2023 (National Semiconductor, Digi-Key).
- **Some makers round to a six-week block.** National Semiconductor's 0012 means week 12 to 17 of 2000. Three digits are YWW, two are YW. One letter is a six-week block in a three-year span.
- **Capacitors (Vishay):** a year letter, then a month character. Other makers differ, so check the datasheet.
- Year letters: F 2015, H 2016, J 2017, K 2018, L 2019, M 2020, N 2021, P 2022, R 2023, S 2024, T 2025, U 2026, V 2027, W 2028, X 2029, A 2030.
- Month: 1 to 9 are Jan to Sep. O or A is Oct. N or B is Nov. D or C is Dec. "U2" is Feb 2026.
- The IEC 60062 letters repeat every 20 years. So A is also 2010 and F is also 1995.
- Other Vishay series print YYWW. 2544 is week 44 of 2025 (Vishay).
- A code is when the **part** was made, not the device. Read several parts and take the newest. Part numbers can look like dates: a 7805 is a regulator (Digi-Key).
- Brand serial-number decoding is left out. No reliable public source was confirmed.

## Dates that change what is inside
| Item | Date | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Leaded solder | EU, **1 July 2006** | RoHS: new EU-market equipment may not contain lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB or PBDE. Exempt: solder over 85 % lead, some network gear (EUR-Lex). It follows the sale date, not chip dates. Older or non-EU gear may be leaded. |
| R-12 (CFC-12) in cars | Early to mid 1990s | R-134a replaced R-12 in new cars. US production and import of CFCs ended **1 Jan 1996** (EPA). |
| R-12 in fridges | Before 1995 | Fridges and freezers made before 1995 usually hold CFC. After 1995, HFC. Foam made before 2005 holds ozone-depleting gas (EPA). |
| R-600a (isobutane) | Abroad since about the mid-1990s. New US fridges from **21 Feb 2012** | Used in Germany, the UK, Australia and Japan for over 15 years by 2011. **Flammable.** US limit is 57 g per sealed system. Marked with flammable-refrigerant labels (Federal Register). |
| PCB capacitors | US ban **1979** | Ballasts made before 2 July 1979 may hold PCBs. Non-PCB ballasts made 1 July 1978 to 1 July 1998 had to say "No PCBs". Unmarked, undated pre-1979 capacitors: assume PCBs. Motor and compressor capacitors too (EPA). |
| Mercury switches | Some fridges and chests before 2000. Some cars before 2003 | Also old thermostats, flame sensors, and tilt switches in washers and freezer lids. A magnetic sensor is often mercury (EPA). In a thermostat, glass vials with silver liquid are mercury (Vermont DEC). |
| Ionisation smoke alarm | No date found | Holds americium-241, half-life 432 years (CDC). A radiation symbol, "Am-241", "ionization" or "microcurie" on the label means yes. Never open it. Photoelectric-only units hold none (LANL). |
| CRT glass | Any CRT TV or colour monitor | Average 4 lb (1.8 kg) of lead each (EPA). Do not break the tube. |
| Asbestos | Older appliances | Wiring and insulation in furnaces and stoves (EPA). Older stove-top pads, ironing-board covers and some hair dryers (CPSC). CPSC acted on hair dryers in May 1979. Do not saw, sand, drill or sweep it (CPSC). |
| Cadmium (NiCd) | EU laws due **26 Sept 2008**. Power tools **31 Dec 2016** | EU limit is 0.002 % cadmium in portable batteries. Cordless tools were exempt until 31 Dec 2016 (EUR-Lex). The US law of 13 May 1996 requires "Ni-Cd" and a recycle mark (Congress). |

## Handling rules
- Do not vent refrigerant. It is illegal under US Clean Air Act section 608 (EPA).
- Do not cut or braze a sealed system you cannot identify. It may hold flammable R-600a.
- Spilled mercury: do not sweep or vacuum. Ventilate, isolate the room and stay out for 15 minutes (Vermont DEC).
